content: If any contacts develop symptoms, the alert system must be activated immediately. Designated areas such as Transit/Isolation Units or Community Care Centers (CCCs) should be established for isolating individuals who meet the criteria for a suspected Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) case. While separate facilities can be created, existing infrastructure, such as airports, border posts, and healthcare facilities, can also be utilized. Suspected EVD cases awaiting confirmation will require access to food, potable water, and basic necessities. In some cases, blood samples for EVD testing may be collected in the transit or isolation unit, and individuals may need to remain there until test results are available. If initial testing occurs within three days of symptom onset, a new blood sample must be obtained 72 hours after symptom onset to confirm the absence of EVD. It is preferable to have an in-country laboratory capable of EVD testing. If this is not feasible, a nearby laboratory that can provide rapid results must be identified. Planners should evaluate the availability of necessary equipment, including reagents, the biosafety level of the laboratory, and the presence of adequately trained staff. Ebola Treatment Units or Centers (ETUs/ETCs), or CCCs in some cases, are facilities where probable or confirmed EVD cases receive treatment. In certain settings, suspected and probable EVD cases are immediately transferred to ETUs/ETCs, where blood samples are drawn, and they await test results. These facilities are specifically designed to prevent the transmission of EVD to others and must adhere to WHO guidelines. At least one ETU/ETC should be operational before the first EVD case is detected in the country. A dedicated data manager should oversee the entry and management of all data, including the daily follow-up of contacts. If contacts are spread across multiple districts, a data manager may be required in each district. A system for collecting, managing, and analyzing data should be established. Electronic data entry is recommended for faster data exchange, immediate reporting to key stakeholders, and mandatory reporting to WHO. If electronic systems are unavailable, paper-based data management can be used, with standardized forms and strict enforcement of data field completion. Under the incident management framework, various teams are required to coordinate the response to identify, control, and eliminate EVD. These teams include the Contact Tracing Team, Case Management Team, Social Mobilization Team, Laboratory Team, and Logistics Team. Effective communication between these teams, facilitated by team leads, is essential. Suggested qualifications and responsibilities for team members, including those in related teams such as Transportation, Disinfection, and Burial Teams, should be adapted to the local context. Resources for training personnel are also provided. Resources and equipment must be procured and ready for distribution to the Investigation Team and for initial response activities. While scalability should be considered, the primary focus should be on resources required for the initial response to avoid delays in intervention. A sample minimum equipment list is available as a guide. Resource requirements will vary by country, depending on existing infrastructure and available resources. A common barrier to rapid response during the identification of initial EVD cases is the lack of discretionary funds or authority to release funds immediately. Delays in response activities, even by a few hours, can result in significant transmission chains. Funding must be allocated during preparation activities and before the first EVD case is detected. Budgetary considerations for initiating a rapid response are provided, with resource needs varying by country based on existing infrastructures and financial status. Contact tracing can only interrupt the chain of EVD transmission if implemented immediately upon identifying a suspected, probable, or confirmed EVD case. Laboratory confirmation should not delay the initiation of contact tracing. Upon detecting a potential EVD case, an Investigation Team should be mobilized immediately to assess the individual for EVD symptoms, exposure type, and risk factors. If the individual meets the EVD case definition, the Incident Management Framework is activated. The Investigation Team, working with the Case Management Team, should interview the EVD case to systematically identify all potential contacts since the onset of symptoms. This interview must be comprehensive and detailed, covering all activities and individuals involved since the illness began. If the case is unable to communicate or has died, the team should gather information from family members, caregivers, and others involved in the case’s routine activities or events leading to their identification as a case. The team must visit the household of each case and any healthcare facilities visited by the case. They should verify and double-check exposure information for consistency and completeness during follow-up visits to ensure all contacts and potential transmission chains are identified. Failure to identify even a single contact may result in ongoing EVD transmission. All individuals, including the case, their family, and close contacts, should have an easy way to reach the Investigation Team if they recall additional contacts after the interview. A step-by-step procedure outline is available. Laboratory confirmation should not delay contact tracing initiation. Interviews should be conducted in a safe and conducive environment to establish trust and rapport with the case, family, and community. Probing questions should be culturally sensitive and focus on the period when the case developed symptoms. If the case is a healthcare worker, all patients and colleagues of the healthcare worker should be identified. If the case has died, all individuals who had contact with the deceased, including funeral attendees, should be identified. A calendar or specific dates, such as local holidays, may help potential cases recall activities. Psychosocial support staff on the Investigation Team can reassure the case and facilitate contact identification. During initial contact tracing, splitting the Investigation Team into groups focusing on healthcare and community contacts may be helpful, but strong communication between teams is essential. Identifying all contacts can be logistically challenging, and solutions may include engaging community leaders or using cell phone companies to track contacts via GPS. Any person meeting the contact definition criteria should be listed as a contact using the Contact Listing Form. Information about the contact’s relationship to the case, date of last interaction, and type of interaction should be collected, along with their address and telephone number if available. The Investigation Team should personally identify and interview every listed contact, asking about their last interaction with the case. If discrepancies arise, the most recent date since the case’s symptom onset should be used as the start of the 21-day follow-up period. Contacts should be informed of their risk status, the follow-up plan, and educated about EVD signs, symptoms, and preventive measures. They should understand the importance of early clinical care and immediate isolation to reduce the risk of infecting others. If a contact develops symptoms, they should self-isolate and notify the team to prevent further transmission. Symptomatic contacts are potential suspected EVD cases and should be transported to a transit or isolation unit for further testing. Contact identification and listing should begin for any new suspected EVD case. The first meeting with a contact is critical for building trust and should ideally involve an epidemiologist and psychosocial support staff. The Contact Follow-up Team assigned to the contact should be introduced during this meeting to foster trust and continuity. Daily visits by the Contact Follow-up Team should evaluate the contact’s health status through direct observation and questions about their well-being and fever. This information should be recorded on the Daily Contact Follow-up Form. Contacts with symptoms should not have their temperature taken by the team. The team should also inquire about any unwell individuals in the household to identify potential cases in the community. If a contact is absent, the team should determine their location and report all findings to their Supervisor at the end of each day.
